note: Cross-layer money cases (#6). Read by frontend/src/lib/format.test.ts AND backend/tests/test_currency.py, so an amount that means one thing in the browser and another in Python fails a test instead of reaching the database. Add a case here rather than to either suite. `why` is for the reader; nothing asserts on it.

minor_fraction_digits.why: CLDR says 0; ISO 4217 says 3, and storage follows ISO
CLDR says 0 — an ordinary currency the two layers used to disagree about
unrecognised: the documented default, not an error

major_to_minor.why: grouped with no decimal point — still unambiguous
the zero-digit currency where a grouped integer is the normal way to write money
no minor unit to hold the half — rounds, and the form now says so
half away from zero; the float route gave 100
the headline case — used to import as 123
<input type=number> passes exponent notation through verbatim
below half — genuinely zero, not a parse failure

major_to_minor_refused.why: #40. A comma was stripped unconditionally, so '12,34' — how much of the world writes 12.34 — became 1234 major units and stored a hundredfold error. These are the inputs neither layer may guess at. The two signal it differently and that is fine: the backend raises (a cell gets a row diagnostic and the import stops), the browser returns 0 (a form field visibly empties instead of silently multiplying by 100). What must not differ is WHICH inputs are refused.

cases.why: the headline case — a European decimal comma
fully European: grouped by point, decimal by comma
four digits after the comma is no grouping anyone uses
two digits — the shape of a decimal comma
an inconsistent group in the middle
Decimal() honours Python literal underscores; the sheet said no such number

round_trips.why: Every amount against every currency: export writes major units and import reads them back, so the pair has to land on the integer it started from. Expressed as a product rather than a list so adding one currency covers all the awkward amounts at once.
